prompt.context: Our client is a major supermarket chain in Canada. They are one of three major players in this sector and the rest of the market is split amongst smaller, regional firms. In January 2000, they introduced a loyalty card scheme run by a third party provider, but have not been able to make this scheme successful. The CEO has called us in to review their program and suggest ways to improve it.
prompt.question: What areas should we investigate to determine the performance of this scheme, and how can the client improve it?

clarifying_info.q: How does the loyalty card work?
clarifying_info.a: For every $1 spent in store, the customer receives 1 point. These points can be redeemed for discounts at the store. 100 points can be redeemed for a 1% saving on every $100 spent.

clarifying_info.q: Who runs the loyalty card program?
clarifying_info.a: The program is run by a third party provider.

clarifying_info.q: How many total transactions are there?

exhibits.title: Transaction data for loyalty cardholders and non-loyalty cardholders
exhibits.shows: A stacked bar chart comparing the percentage of transactions and percentage of spend for loyalty card holders versus non-loyalty card holders. Total spend is $300MM.

exhibits.title: Number of supermarket loyalty cards in wallet
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing the distribution of how many supermarket loyalty cards customers carry in their wallet (0, 1, 2, or 3). The distribution is bimodal.

data.shape: bimodal — peaks at 0 cards and at 3 cards

framework: Define goals of the scheme: profitability, business intelligence, or customer retention
Benchmark potential profitability: compare to competitors' schemes or grocery stores in other regions
Assess current profitability vs. benchmark: identify any gap and its drivers
Analyze cost structure of running the program (discounts, third-party fees, promotion, software, support)
Evaluate actual customer loyalty: do card holders truly shop more exclusively at this chain?
Consider alternatives: other pricing, promotion, or customer loyalty schemes

questions.prompt: What areas should we investigate to determine the performance of the loyalty card scheme?
questions.guidance: A strong answer identifies: (1) scheme goals (profitability vs. intelligence), (2) benchmarking against competitors or other regions, (3) profitability analysis (total customers x % with card x extra profit per customer, driven by visit frequency and spend per visit), and (4) consideration of alternatives. The profitability framework should be: Total customers * % customers with card * extra profits generated per customer.

questions.prompt: What are the costs associated with running a loyalty card program?
questions.guidance: Strong answer covers: (1) Discounts — the largest cost; (2) Software upgrades to registers; (3) Promotion of the scheme; (4) Customer support; (5) Printing cards and maintaining data — likely borne by the third party provider and paid on a per-customer rate; (6) Management and consulting fees. Candidate should keep in mind that a third party provider is running this program.

questions.prompt: (a) How would you interpret Exhibit 1 (transaction data)? (b) Calculate the average revenue per transaction for loyalty card holders and for non-loyalty card holders.
questions.guidance: (a) A large share of transactions are from non-loyalty customers, suggesting many customers are unaware of or not enrolled in the scheme — potential to grow. Loyalty card holders appear to spend more per transaction, but causality is unclear: high-frequency shoppers may self-select into the card, or the card may drive higher spend. (b) Loyalty spend per transaction = $36; non-loyalty spend per transaction = $27.

math.setup: Spend per transaction = (Total spend * % spend) / (Total transactions * % transactions). Total spend = $300MM, Total transactions = 10MM. Loyalty: 40% of spend, 1/3 of transactions. Non-loyalty: 60% of spend, 2/3 of transactions.
math.answer: Loyalty card holders: $36/transaction; Non-loyalty card holders: $27/transaction

questions.prompt: Exhibit 2 shows a bimodal distribution of loyalty cards carried per customer. What does this tell you?
questions.guidance: Most customers either have no loyalty cards or carry cards for all three major supermarkets (one for each major chain). This means loyalty cards do not in fact encourage loyalty to a particular chain — customers carry all available cards and use the appropriate one wherever they shop. A small segment is unaware of or indifferent to all schemes. Key insight: loyalty cards likely determine what products or how much someone buys at a given store, not where they choose to shop.

brainstorming.prompt: How can the client improve its loyalty card program?

categories.name: Enrollment and awareness
ideas: Run promotional campaigns to enroll more card members
Increase in-store and out-of-store marketing of the scheme
Partner with the third-party provider to target non-enrolled high-frequency customers

categories.name: Reward structure redesign
ideas: Give additional loyalty points for high-margin products to steer purchasing
Restructure the formula to provide dollar-amount discounts on specific high-margin items
Offer tiered rewards to incentivize higher total spend levels

categories.name: Alternative approaches
ideas: Consider targeted coupons or personalized promotions using transaction data
Explore coalitions with non-competing retailers to increase card value
Evaluate whether the third-party provider arrangement is optimal or if in-house management would reduce costs

recommendation: The loyalty card scheme has potential but is underperforming due to low enrollment and a reward structure that does not drive true store loyalty

Recommend: (1) Launch enrollment campaigns to grow the cardholder base; (2) Restructure rewards to concentrate points/discounts on high-margin products; (3) Use transaction data for targeted promotions
risks: Competitors may respond with improved schemes, limiting competitive advantage
Increased discount costs on high-margin items may erode margins if not carefully calibrated
Third-party provider constraints may limit flexibility in restructuring the reward formula
next_steps: Quantify the enrollment gap and model the revenue impact of closing it
Analyze margin data by product category to identify optimal products for bonus points
Negotiate with the third-party provider on flexibility to restructure rewards and reduce per-customer fees
